doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Mixing as subtractive; drums and piano under vocals
summary: He describes miking drums, listening to overheads first, mixing by removal, and pulling the piano back a dB under a vocal.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: sharpener, yeah I think we can do this. These are the tools, let’s do it. And I love that challenge of going into a new room, new for me, and making that happen. And you don’t often have the opportunity when there’s an 18-piece big band and you’ve, “Yeah let me hear a little bit of this and that” and you just have the sections play a little bit just to make sure that they’re all fine with ears and whatnot, and then it’s like, “Okay well let’s try one.” And someone counts it off and like at the end of four you’re just like, “Mommy!” because you don’t know what’s going to hit you. And then just that roar of sound of everyone playing together is just fantastic. You get that now at SNL if I get a good band and they start playing the first thing down when it’s just all coming together is great. That’s another thing, when you’re doing SNL and we have monitors for everyone in the band whether or not it’s in-ears or wedges and PA, it has to happen for the studio audience. That’s when the drums can be a little tedious. Like let’s hear the kick drum. Okay let me hear the next thing. You know? But if I’m in a studio I’ll make friends with the drummer by putting the mics where I want them. I’ll say, first of all, “Is anything in your way? Are you going to hit anything?” “No it all looks fine.” I said, “Okay.” That 20- minute solo they’re not going to let you put on the record, I’ll listen to it now thank you, and just start playing and I’ll just start molding and getting in there and doing what I need and deciding yes I do have that mic but I don’t think I need it. Always listen to the overheads first to hear whether or not someone is going, you know, snare-hat-tom tom tom-snare-hat. Or they’re playing a unified kit. And that will become readily apparent, especially if you’re using like a coincident pair of things. And you know as I used to say, and the same thing with mixing, how do you carve an elephant out of a block of marble? You just chip away everything that doesn’t look like the elephant. So for me with the mix it’s just slowly molding things into place. Tucking this in, pulling this out a bit, making this fit next to this better. It’s all a very — it’s very tactile and it’s also very subtractive as in why don’t I hear — well I’ll throw this in for you — why don’t I hear the ocarina? Or maybe something’s in the way, or I actually need more of it. But if you can’t hear something, if you start, “Well I need more this, more this, and all of a sudden all your faders are up to the wood and you have nowhere to go. Mixing to me is very subtractive. See what’s in the way of something first, whether or not it’s a frequency thing, whether or not it’s a level thing. It could even be a placement thing within the stereo field. And all of a sudden this opens up and this becomes a little easier to hear. I mean this is all because I’ve been doing this for a while, it’s not that — you know the deep fried turkey thing, you’ve watched one too many people put the turkey in, and you go to yourself, “I’m not doing that.” So you begin to learn from your own mistakes, disasters, what have you. I’ve done things on SNL where it’s just — and even in the studio — where it’s just piano and vocal. Let’s just say it’s that. I will take the piano and just breathe on it to stay

out of the way of the vocalist. Just work with the level. I don’t want to do anything to the innate dynamics of the vocalist. They’ve got that. But if I feel from where I’m sitting that the pianist is maybe digging in a little bit too much and I’m losing the vocal I would sooner pull the piano back just a dB or something so that the vocal, there’s never any percept slight change, however imperceptive of what that vocalist is doing. Again, it works for me. It’s just a methodology that I’ve developed and —
